az_cracker_jack_cliffs.blurb: Cracker Jack Cliffs is one sector of the Jacks Canyon sport crag, a short drive south of Winslow. The rock is steep and heavily pocketed, a mix of limestone and sandier stone, and nearly everything here is bolted. The bulk of the climbing sits in the 5.10 to 5.12 range, with a handful of easier lines and a few harder ones, so it suits climbers who already lead the low double digits. Enemy Wind and Firedance are among the better-known lines. This sector takes a lot of sun and can feel scorching on a warm day, so shadier walls elsewhere in the canyon are the better choice in heat, while winter sun makes it pleasant when it is cold. Spring and fall are the comfortable seasons.
az_cracker_jack_cliffs.parking_note: Drive south from Winslow and turn onto the dirt road leading to the rim of Jacks Canyon. The primitive campground along the rim doubles as the parking area for the sectors below.
az_cracker_jack_cliffs.approach: Walk to the canyon rim from the campground and follow the trail down to the base of the wall; the descent is short, roughly a ten-minute walk.

az_pinnacle_peak_2.blurb: Pinnacle Peak is a granite summit in the middle of a city park in north Scottsdale, and one of the Phoenix area's traditional granite outcrops. Climbing here is mostly trad, with cracks and thinner, footwork-driven faces, plus a few bolted lines and a couple of aid routes. Grades spread from beginner-friendly up through 5.11 and a little beyond, with the heaviest concentration around 5.10 to 5.11. Because it sits in a busy hiking park, expect foot traffic on the trail and plan around desert heat.
az_pinnacle_peak_2.parking_note: Use the Pinnacle Peak Park trailhead lot on N. 102nd Way in north Scottsdale.
az_pinnacle_peak_2.approach: From the trailhead, follow the main park trail and look for the spur marked for climbing access, which leads to the peak from the east. Another way is to take the wide cart path from the visitor center to the first climbers' trail sign, then head up and left toward the peak.

az_grail_the.blurb: The Grail is the showpiece wall of Lime Kiln Canyon, in the Arizona Strip just across the line from Mesquite, Nevada. It is a tall, vertical to slightly overhanging limestone face covered in square-cut holds, and every route here is sport. The climbing runs from 5.10 up to 5.13 with a fat middle of 5.12s, so it rewards climbers who are comfortable on sustained, steep pitches. Many routes are long, with a mid-height anchor that lets you stop and lower on a single rope, and a 70 m rope is useful for the full lengths. The wall faces north and stays shaded, which keeps it cool and sometimes chilly early in the day. Space at the base is tight, so keep gear compact.
az_grail_the.parking_note: Reached by a long dirt road from the Mesquite area; the last stretch is rough and high clearance is a big help.
az_grail_the.approach: A steady uphill hike from the parking area, keeping the wall on your right, takes roughly twenty minutes.

az_upper_sullie_s_south_side.blurb: This is a section of Upper Sullivan's Canyon near Prescott, a steep canyon of dark, columnar basalt that is among the area's best-known crack climbing spots. Nearly everything here is traditional protection, with a few top-rope lines on the shorter cliffs. Most of the grades fall between 5.8 and 5.10, with a scattering of easier cracks and a few 5.11s, which makes it a friendly place to learn to place gear and jam. Coffin Crack, S Crack and Nice Hands are well-liked lines. The cliffs are shorter than in the lower canyon, so it works well for a relaxed day of cracks and top-roping.

az_ravens_the.blurb: The Ravens are a cluster of four towers on the hillside near the top of Mount Lemmon, above Summerhaven at roughly 9,000 feet. Most of the climbing is sport, with some trad, and the routes are long and sustained for the mountain, often 100 to 200 feet, the length set by which face of a tower you choose. The grades concentrate in the 5.10 to 5.12 range, with 5.11 the most common. Because the towers face different directions, shade is usually available on one side or another, and the altitude keeps things cool. The approach is long by Lemmon standards, and afternoon storms with lightning can build, so start early and keep an eye on the sky.
az_ravens_the.parking_note: From the top of the Catalina Highway, drive past the ski area and through the gate, then park in the gravel lot on the left before the observatory.
az_ravens_the.approach: Walk around the fenced transformers and follow the old fire lookout road downhill. Continue about 300 yards beyond the Summerhaven water pumphouse and turn left at an electrical box where the road bends right, then head to whichever side of the towers holds your route.

az_boneyard.blurb: The Boneyard is a mid-mountain sport crag on Mount Lemmon, near the Catalina Highway at roughly 7,800 feet. The climbing is more feature-driven than the crimpy style found elsewhere on the mountain, with corners, aretes, roofs and slabs. Almost every route is bolted, and the grades cluster at 5.10 and 5.11 with a few easier and a few harder. Many lines are long, so bring a 70 m rope and tie a stopper knot in the end. The wall gets sun in the morning and the right side goes into shade by late morning, which makes it a good escape from low-elevation heat. Newer lines can be dirty; heavy lichen usually means you have drifted off route. It sits close to the road, which makes retreating from a storm easy.
az_boneyard.parking_note: Use the right-hand pullout near milepost 18.5 on the Catalina Highway, beside a white rock quarry. Other cars there may belong to climbers visiting a neighboring crag.
az_boneyard.approach: Take the trail up the steep slope at the top of the lot and follow a drainage wash with polished, slippery slabs. At the saddle go right to reach the base. It takes about fifteen minutes.

az_dws_east_side.blurb: This is the east side of the deep water soloing walls along East Clear Creek, near Winslow. Coconino sandstone cliffs rise straight from deep water, and the stone grips well even with wet shoes. Most of what is here is bouldering and soloing over water, from easy low problems to more serious solo lines, plus a few short trad routes. Getting to the walls takes a boat or paddle craft along a stretch of creek, and wind can make paddling tiring. Swimming ability is required, and landing zones can be shallow or change after floods, so check the depth before each attempt and never dive in from a climb. Summer heat is the main draw, since the water offers relief.
az_dws_east_side.parking_note: From Winslow take Hwy 87 south, turn left onto Hwy 99 and drive about five miles to McHood Park. Park in the park and launch your boat there.
